title: Explain it, and say how sure you are
outcomes: Commits to an answer and a confidence before seeing feedback
Explains in two sentences why a move works and compares with checked facts

steps.text: **Explain, and say how sure you are.** Before you see an answer, commit to it and rate your confidence: low, medium or high. Afterwards compare. Over many answers you can see whether your 'high' is right more often than your 'low'. That match is called *calibration*. It is a habit to try; evidence for it in chess is thin.

steps.title: Confidence and evidence
steps.prompt: Answer each position and mark your confidence (low, medium or high) before you check. Then compare confidence with the result.

steps.text: Look at your three answers. A confident wrong answer (the trap) teaches more than a lucky right one. If your 'high' answers are wrong about one time in four or more, treat 'high' as 'check once more'. That cut-off is a guess, not a measured threshold.

steps.prompt: Count from the table the app shows after the contrast, or from your own answers. This is for you, not a grade.

fields.label: Of those, how many were right:
Of those, how many were right:
What pattern do you see, if any?

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Now it shows your confidence table straight after the contrast and gives feedback after each item. In the next two items, a silent session, feedback waits until you have answered both. The plan is to show the table only on request after five sessions (a first guess).

steps.prompt: Teach-back. Pick one of the positions from this lesson. In two sentences, explain to a beginner why the best move works. Then compare your sentences with the checked explanation shown for the item and note what you missed.

fields.label: What the checked explanation had that I left out:
How sure was I before checking?
